item.title: 1: Daily Halacha: Adar & Fate
item.description:
When Adar begins we increase our happiness, and the Talmud says Israel has better mazal then, though elsewhere it says ein mazal leYisrael. The Ibn Ezra explains that one who lives with Hashem is above fate, and Adar helps only those who live under it. The Meiri explains the joy: in the Megillah Hashem's hand is hidden, and learning to see Him in everything, good and bad, is what fills a person with simhah.
Daily Halacha — Purim Dayan Daniel Kada

item.title: 2: Daily Halacha: What Does It Mean to Be Happy in Adar?
item.description:
What does the saying that when Adar begins we increase joy mean? It parallels the Mishnah in Taanit that joy is reduced when Av begins, and the Rambam and Shulhan Arukh codify that one. The Rabbi explains one reading, in connection with reading the Megillah, and promises a second tomorrow.

item.title: 3: Daily Halacha: Happiness in Adar
item.description:
Does increasing joy at the start of Adar mean doing something? The Rambam and Shulhan Arukh omit Mishenikhnas Adar Marbim BeSimhah. The Meiri says it is not literal. One approach is a shift of outlook, seeing HaShem behind everything in daily life, which naturally increases joy. Next: mazal and Adar.

item.title: 5: Daily Halacha: Mahasit HaShekel Part 1: Introduction to the Custom
item.description:
In the time of the Beit HaMikdash every Jew gave half a shekel each year for the daily korban tamid, collected from Rosh Hodesh Adar, which is why we read Parashat Shekalim. The custom of giving half a coin before Purim first appears in Masekhet Soferim, from the time of the Geonim; it is not in the Rambam or the Shulhan Arukh, but the Rema records it and Sefaradim later adopted it. It is a minhag, not one of the four misvot of Purim, and may be given from the first of Adar.
Daily Halacha — Purim Dayan Daniel Kada

item.title: 6: Daily Halacha: Mahasit HaShekel Part 2: How Much to Give and Who Is Obligated to Give
item.description:
How much is given for Mahasit HaShekel, and on whose behalf? The Rema's custom for Ashkenazim is half a local coin, often three of them, while Sefaradim give the value of nine grams of silver, about five pounds forty. Strictly it applies to men from twenty, or thirteen, but the custom is to give for one's wife, children and even an unborn child, and Rav Ovadia Yosef says not to overstretch for a minhag.
Daily Halacha — Purim Dayan Daniel Kada

item.title: 7: Daily Halacha: Mahasit HaShekel Part 3: More Details
item.description:
May maaser money be used for Mahasit HaShekel? Rav Ovadia Yosef says not, unless one began giving maaser beli neder, without a vow. The money may go to the synagogue or to the poor, but it does not count towards matanot laevyonim on Purim day, and one should not call it the half shekel itself, only a zekher, a remembrance of it.
Daily Halacha — Purim Dayan Daniel Kada

item.title: 8: Daily Halacha: Parashat Zakhor: Why, How, When & Women
item.description:
The misvah to remember Amalek must be said aloud, by reading the verses of Parashat Zakhor; some require a Sefer Torah, others are satisfied with a Humash. Most hold it is once a year and need not be this Shabbat, so one who cannot attend can read it at home now and hear it from the Torah in Parashat Ki Tese. The Sefer HaHinukh exempts women, since the misvah is tied to waging war, though they should hear it if they can.
Daily Halacha — Purim Dayan Daniel Kada

item.title: 9: Daily Halacha: Parashat Zakhor: Amalek and Doubt
item.description:
Why does Amalek stand for the danger of doubt? Shelomoh HaMelech's picture in Mishlei of the evil fool, who casts doubt on everything, connects to Amalek, whose name has the same letters as ulai. For Parashat Zakhor: we remember Amalek because the philosophy of doubt remains, and the answer is commitment to truth.

item.title: 10: Daily Halacha: Waging War Against Amalek Nowadays
item.description:
Is there still a misvah to wage war against Amalek? Most Rishonim say it waits for the days of Mashiah, since Amalek can no longer be identified, and the Hafes Hayim calls it all or nothing. The Rambam holds that a descendant of Amalek who makes peace, or even accepts the seven Noahide laws, is accepted, but the misvot to remember and not to forget still apply.

item.title: 11: Daily Halacha: How We Remember Amalek Nowadays and Different Pronunciations
item.description:
How do we fulfil the misvah of remembering Amalek today? It is a verbal misvah done once a year on Shabbat Zakhor; Tosafot require reading from a Sefer Torah with a minyan, while the Rambam holds one fulfils it even reading alone from a Humash. There is no need to hear it in every pronunciation, only in one's own family tradition, and women are strictly not obligated, since the misvah is tied to waging war.
Daily Halacha — Purim Dayan Daniel Kada

item.title: 12: Daily Halacha: Purim: The Root of Anti-Semitism
item.description:
Why is the Torah so severe about Amalek, more than about Egypt? Amalek attacked a nation of freed slaves without provocation and is the root of all hatred of the Jewish people, so the Torah commands us to remember, not to forget, and to wipe them out. Shaul's misplaced compassion for Agag let Amalek survive, and from Agag came Haman: compassion taken to an extreme can allow further attacks.
Daily Halacha — Purim Dayan Daniel Kada

item.title: 13: Daily Halacha: The Fast of Esther
item.description:
Taanit Esther is not one of the fasts of the Prophets but a custom first recorded in the time of the Geonim, which all Israel has accepted, as the Rambam writes. Because it is lighter than the other fasts, pregnant and nursing women, the very elderly, a hatan in his seven days, the father, sandak and mohel at a brit, and anyone in real pain need not fast. We fast not because Esther fasted but because the Jews fasted when they went out to battle on the 13th of Adar, so it is not a sad day.
Daily Halacha — Purim Dayan Daniel Kada

item.title: 14: Daily Halacha: Brit This Coming Thursday
item.description:
What happens when a brit milah falls on the Fast of Esther, brought forward this year to Thursday? The fast is a minhag recalling the day the Jews went out to battle, not a tragedy, which is why it is brought forward rather than postponed. The Rema allows not only the father, sandak and mohel but all the guests to eat at the brit meal, though the guests must then fast on Friday, and even a slight illness exempts one from this fast.
Daily Halacha — Purim Dayan Daniel Kada

item.title: 15: Daily Halacha: Why Two Days of Purim?
item.description:
Why are there two days of Purim? The Jews of Shushan fought for an extra day and rested on the 15th, so walled cities keep Shushan Purim, but walled since the days of Yehoshua rather than the time of the story, so that Jerusalem, then in ruins, would be included. A walled city like York keeps the 14th, and one who keeps Purim in Ashdod and is in Jerusalem at dawn on the 15th must keep it all again.
Daily Halacha — Purim Dayan Daniel Kada

item.title: 16: Daily Halacha: Skipping Purim
item.description:
Purim falls on the 14th of Adar, and on the 15th, Shushan Purim, in cities walled since the days of Yehoshua, so where a person is at dawn decides which day he keeps. Travelling into Jerusalem can oblige him to keep both days, and travelling out at the right time can mean keeping neither. Places of doubt such as Tiberias and Yafo keep the 15th as well, without the berakhah on the Megillah.
Daily Halacha — Purim Dayan Daniel Kada

item.title: 17: Daily Halacha: Doubts in Misvot from the נביאים
item.description:
Is a doubt about the Megillah to be treated leniently or strictly? Since the misvah comes from the prophets (divrei kabbalah), many Rishonim and poskim treat it like a rabbinic misvah and lean lenient. The Mishnah Berurah is stringent for the day reading, and for the night reading all agree one may be lenient.

item.title: 18: Daily Halacha: The Misvot of Purim
item.description:
Mishloah manot is two ready-to-eat foods to one person, given by day; matanot laevyonim is two gifts to two poor people, each about the cost of a basic meal, and the Rambam says to spend more on the poor than on mishloah manot. Gifts may be collected in advance but must reach the poor on Purim day. The seudah is held only by day, since the threat at Purim was physical, unlike Hanukkah.
Daily Halacha — Purim Dayan Daniel Kada

item.title: 19: Daily Halacha: The Obligation of Reading the Megillah at Night and Day
item.description:
The Megillah must be read both at night and by day, and the daytime reading, instituted by Mordekhai and Esther, is the main one, while the night reading is rabbinic. So one who can hear only one reading should choose the day. Sefaradim say Shehehiyanu only at night, while the Rema has Ashkenazim say it again by day.

item.title: 20: Daily Halacha: Women Reading the Megillah
item.description:
May a woman read the Megillah for a man? Most Rishonim allow it, since both are obligated and reading is not singing, while others object that her obligation is only to hear, or that it reflects badly on the community. The Shulhan Arukh allows it in case of need, which is better than hearing it over Zoom, and a woman reading for other women, even a group, is the custom in many communities.

item.title: 21: Daily Halacha: Hearing the Megillah Over the Telephone
item.description:
Can one fulfil the misvah of hearing the Megillah over the telephone? Rav Shlomo Zalman Auerbach, followed by Rav Ovadia Yosef, says no, since a mechanically reproduced voice is not a human voice. Rav Moshe Feinstein says yes, since every voice reaches us as sound waves, and Rav Frank, Chief Rabbi of Jerusalem, agrees for a different reason: hearing the result of a human voice is enough.

item.title: 22: Daily Halacha: Hearing the Megillah Over Zoom
item.description:
Does Rav Moshe Feinstein's leniency for hearing the Megillah by telephone extend to Zoom, with its many more steps? Rav Frank's view would allow it and the strict view would not, so the order of preference is in person, then telephone, then Zoom. The daytime reading, from the Prophets, outweighs the rabbinic night reading, so one who can go out only once should go by day.

item.title: 23: Daily Halacha: The Love of the Megillah
item.description:
Because the Megillah is so beloved, the halacha makes three exceptions for it. It may be read after midnight even at the outset, it may be heard from several readers at once though two voices normally cannot be followed, and mistakes in reading it are treated more leniently than in the Torah reading.

item.title: 24: Daily Halacha: The Megillah & the Theme of Kavod
item.description:
What is the theme running through the Megillah? Kavod: Ahasuerus and Vashti, then Haman and Mordekhai, each fighting over honour, power and money, which cannot be shared. The pursuit of truth can be shared, which is why Mordekhai and Esther can work together.

item.title: 25: Daily Halacha: The Reasons for Mishloach Manot
item.description:
Why do we give mishloah manot? One reason is so that everyone has enough food for the Purim seudah, the other is to build the friendship that answers Haman's charge of a scattered people. The two reasons divide over a gift refused at the door and one given anonymously, so in both cases the gift should be repeated to someone who accepts it and knows who sent it.

item.title: 26: Daily Halacha: Is Your Spouse Your Friend?
item.description:
In isolation, can mishloah manot be given within one's own household? Rav Ovadia Yosef rules that a child may give to a parent, just as one may give to one's rav without calling him a friend. Rabbi Akiva Yosef Schlesinger shows from the Gemara that a spouse counts as a rea, so husband and wife may give to each other, with the husband intending the gift to be fully hers, but only when one cannot go out.

item.title: 27: Daily Halacha: When to Have the Purim Seudah This Friday
item.description:
When should the Purim seudah be held when Purim falls on Friday? Strictly it may be held all day, since it is a seudat misvah in its time, but the Rema prefers before midday so that one comes to Shabbat with an appetite. A third option is pores mapah umekadesh: start the meal late in the afternoon, continue into Shabbat, cover the bread and make Kiddush, and say Reseh without Al HaNisim in Birkat HaMazon.

item.title: 31: Daily Halacha: Drunkenness on Purim Day
item.description:
Does the Gemara really require getting drunk on Purim until one cannot tell cursed Haman from blessed Mordekhai? The Rambam and the Meiri explain it as drinking a little more than usual and falling asleep, and the Rema rules this way for Ashkenazim, while the Shulhan Arukh quotes the Gemara as it stands. The drinking belongs only to the Purim seudah, and a person must never lose control or his dignity.

item.title: 32: Daily Halacha: Working on Purim
item.description:
May one work on Purim? The Megillah first speaks of Yom Tov, then only feasting and joy, so work is permitted. Still, the custom is not to do regular work on the day, and one who can refrain should; on Purim night there is no custom to forbid it.

item.title: 33: Daily Halacha: The Murky Origins of Dressing Up on Purim Part 1
item.description:
Where does the custom of dressing up on Purim come from? It is not in the Talmud, the Rambam or the Shulhan Arukh, and is first recorded by Rabbi Yehudah Minz in fifteenth-century Italy. Four reasons are given: the reversals of the Megillah, the dignity of the poor receiving gifts, Amalek disguising themselves as Canaanites, and Hashem hidden behind the story.

item.title: 34: Daily Halacha: The Murky Origins of Dressing Up on Purim Part 2
item.description:
The first source for dressing up on Purim even allows cross-dressing, and the Rema records the custom, but the Rambam and the great majority of poskim forbid it even as a one-off. Rav Yosef Mashash of Haifa traced the custom to the Roman carnival and would allow it only for children. The custom is not banned, but it is a minor part of Purim, and modesty and the normal halachot still apply.

item.title: 35: Daily Halacha: Thirty Days Before Pesah
item.description:
Thirty days before Pesah we begin to study its laws, as Moshe taught Pesah Sheni on Pesah itself, and the halacha is that this applies to everyone, not only rabbis. Why the festival has several names, why the extra Adar keeps it in the spring, and why the Rambam calls these the laws of Hames uMasah. As zeman herutenu, Pesah brought a new idea of freedom: overthrowing masters without enslaving them.
